examples.summary: A small expression language, written in Deed: split into tokens, parse by precedence, evaluate. Tokens are space separated on purpose, to keep character-by-character lexing out of the way of the part this file is actually about, which is precedence and associativity.
Closures, the two holes they used to open, and the boundary they can now cross.
A program that reads a file it was given access to, and cannot read one it was not. `deed run examples/config.deed --dir examples`
A Deed program that actually runs. `deed test examples/counter.deed` executes the tests at the bottom.
Non-termination, which is something a function does, so it goes in the row.
A generator pattern over a Yield effect.
Generic types, and the shortcut they were there to cover for.
Generic functions, and the thing they make possible.
A Deed program with a `main`. `deed run examples/hello.deed` executes it.
Writing a file, which until now the language could not do at all.

A small JSON-shaped value, encoded to text. No decoder: reading JSON back needs a real tokenizer with string-escape handling and a wall this file does not climb, unlike `examples/calculator.deed`'s space-separated shortcut. Left for whoever wants that wall next.

A small key-value store: `key=value` lines, saved and loaded through `Io.save`/`Io.read` the way `journal.deed` and `todo.deed` already do. The parsing and the table-building are pure and tested here; `main` is the untested glue that hands them a real `Dir`, the same split every other example with a `main` already uses.
Holding more than one of something, which until now the language could not do at all.
A program that reads a directory of logs and reports what is in them.

Markdown to plain text, three rules: a line starting `# ` becomes an upper-cased heading, a line starting `- ` becomes an indented bullet, and `**` markers are stripped wherever they appear. Nothing here needs a real Markdown parser (no nesting, no inline links); one line in, one line out, which is as far as `logs.deed`-style line-at-a-time text handling goes before it would need one.
The other side of an import. `deed check examples/` sees this file and `greeting.deed` at the same time, which is what makes the `use` in that file mean something.
The Proven tier, which is the part of this language that is supposed to be interesting.

design/02-syntax.md's stated falsification test for "no traits": write a program needing a generic sort over a user type, or needing to print a `T`, and see whether it is unwritable rather than merely uglier with a passed function.
A cooperative round-robin scheduler, written entirely in Deed.
An effect and a handler, declared here and used from `greeting.deed`.

A tiny stack machine: push a number, or combine the top two with an operator. Four instructions, and the interesting part is `applied`, which is one function for all three binary operators because the operator itself is the parameter, the same shape `logs.deed` uses to take a walk's question as an argument.
Strings, which until recently you could hold and not use.

Tic-tac-toe: a 9-cell board, a move, a winner check over the eight lines that can win, and a text render. The board is a plain `List<String>` rather than a record with nine fields, because every operation here walks it by position and a record would need the same nine-way match `placed` and `rendered` are written once to avoid.
A real program, written to find out what is missing rather than to show off what is there. `deed run examples/todo.deed --dir examples`
The running example, and two of the fourteen design documents work through it: design/02-syntax.md and design/03-effects.md.
A binary search tree, written in Deed.
Using the list library, which is the point of it existing.
A concurrent program written to find the walls.
